summary: Architecture policy for product applications that have outgrown single-folder simplicity but do not need platform-grade ceremony.
description: A portable architecture pack for small-to-mid product applications with multiple features, user workflows, runtime integrations, and enough shared behavior to need explicit boundaries.
plainLanguageSummary: Use this when a product app has several features and needs clear ownership without large-platform ceremony.
bestFor: Small-to-mid product apps with multiple features
Brownfield apps where agents keep creating second patterns
Greenfield apps that need clear feature, infrastructure, shared-code, UI, and generated-output boundaries
notFor: Public libraries where exports are the product
Large modular platforms that need formal package/module ownership
userQuestions: Where does each feature own behavior, UI, and tests?
Which generated files must never be hand-edited?
qualityBar: Rules include examples, anti-patterns, brownfield guidance, greenfield guidance, drift checks, and proof fixtures.
The pack is framework-agnostic and maps roles to local project names instead of forcing folder names.
Agents can explain what to do differently before editing code.
Incomplete heuristics remain advisory until a human confirms the finding.
agentUse: Load this pack after project bootstrap when architecture or file placement matters.
Use accepted local names first, then apply this pack's ownership and dependency direction rules.
Escalate to standard or high-impact risk when changing boundaries, generated outputs, or validation strategies.
Treat all example paths as role evidence, never as required folder names.

structureTree.title: Mid-app structure tree
structureTree.summary: A practical app shape where runtime wiring, product features, infrastructure adapters, shared code, UI primitives, generated outputs, docs, and tests each have a clear owner. These are roles, not required folder names.

nodes.label: App shell and composition root
nodes.responsibility: Owns route setup, app startup, providers, layout shell, and dependency assembly.
antiPatterns: Feature services create database, cache, queue, or API clients directly.

nodes.label: Product features
nodes.responsibility: Owns user workflows, feature services, local components, feature tests, and behavior-specific state.
antiPatterns: Business behavior hidden in generic shared helpers.
One feature imports another feature's private component.

nodes.label: Infrastructure and adapters
nodes.responsibility: Owns API clients, auth/session adapters, environment interpretation, persistence adapters, queue/storage integrations, and vendor boundaries.
antiPatterns: Infrastructure or adapter code imports feature internals.
UI components create infrastructure clients.

nodes.label: Shared code
nodes.responsibility: Owns stable cross-feature helpers, formatting, parsing, small utilities, and project-wide support functions after reuse is proven.
antiPatterns: src/utils/misc.ts becomes a dumping ground.
Shared helpers quietly own product decisions.

nodes.label: Reusable UI primitives
nodes.responsibility: Owns reusable design primitives, page patterns, shells, and low-level UI building blocks that are not feature-specific.
antiPatterns: Feature-specific UI moves into global components before reuse is proven.

nodes.label: Generated outputs
nodes.responsibility: Owns generated SDKs, route maps, schemas, docs indexes, and other files that must be changed through their generator.
antiPatterns: Patch generated output by hand instead of changing the owning source or generator.

nodes.label: Project knowledge
nodes.responsibility: Owns durable project guidance, decisions, architecture notes, and developer-facing explanations.
antiPatterns: Important architecture decisions live only in chat history.

beforeEditing: Identify the current architecture layers before adding files.
Search for existing patterns for routing, services, repositories, validation, config, and generated outputs.
Decide whether this is feature-local, shared code, infrastructure/adapter work, generated-output work, docs, or public-contract work.
beforeReadiness: Confirm no second routing, DI, state, config, validation, or generated-output pattern was introduced.
Confirm changed public contracts have migration notes or explicit user approval.
Confirm verification Guards match the layer touched.

appliesWhen.summary: The project has several feature areas or user workflows that change independently.
evidence: Multiple feature, route, or domain directories

appliesWhen.summary: The project has shared API, persistence, auth, job, storage, or integration code that many features consume.
evidence: Cross-feature imports into helpers or service wrappers

appliesWhen.summary: The project needs more than one verification strategy but does not need a large-platform governance program.
evidence: UI or integration smoke tests are present or planned
Release checks are slower than daily local checks

avoidWhen.summary: A one-off script, spike, or throwaway prototype should not inherit mid-app structure.
A library package with public API compatibility as its main concern should use a library architecture pack instead.
evidence: Semver migration policy dominates feature layout

avoidWhen.summary: A modular platform with strict package boundaries, generated routes, DI, and multi-team ownership needs a large-platform pack.

rules.title: Composition root owns runtime wiring
rules.summary: App startup, route registration, dependency assembly, provider selection, and environment interpretation must live in a composition root or infrastructure/adapters layer, not inside feature internals.
rules.rationale: Feature code stays testable and portable when runtime choices are assembled at the edge.
examples: src/app/** or src/routes/** wires providers and routes
src/infrastructure/**, src/adapters/**, or a local equivalent exposes stable runtime adapters consumed by features
antiPatterns: Feature service imports environment variables directly
UI component creates database/cache/job clients
Route handlers select providers ad hoc

rules.title: Feature owns product behavior
rules.summary: A feature should own its user workflow, domain service, screen-level UI, validation, and local tests unless the behavior is genuinely cross-feature infrastructure.
rules.rationale: Agents can make coherent changes when the behavior they need is locally discoverable.
antiPatterns: Business decisions hidden in shared helpers
Feature UI spread across unrelated global component folders
Tests only at a distant app level

rules.title: Shared code is earned
rules.summary: Shared modules must represent stable cross-feature primitives, infrastructure adapters, or design-system components. Do not create shared buckets for speculative reuse.
rules.rationale: Premature shared folders make agents choose generic placement and create second patterns.
examples: src/shared/formatting/money.ts after two or more features need identical money formatting
src/infrastructure/api/client.ts or src/adapters/api/client.ts as a single API boundary
antiPatterns: src/utils/misc.ts
src/shared/helpers.ts
One feature imports another feature's private helper

rules.title: Import direction is one-way
rules.summary: Feature internals may depend on infrastructure, adapter, shared, or UI primitives, but those lower-level roles must not depend on feature internals, and features must not import private internals from sibling features.
rules.rationale: Acyclic direction keeps refactors bounded and makes ownership clear.
antiPatterns: infrastructure imports features/orders/service
features/billing imports features/orders/components/private-row

rules.title: Public surface is explicit
rules.summary: Feature entrypoints, route handlers, app APIs, and reusable components should expose intentional public files instead of encouraging deep imports.
rules.rationale: Explicit surfaces let agents and humans change internals without breaking unrelated callers.
antiPatterns: Imports from src/features/orders/components/internal/**
Exporting every file through a barrel by default

rules.title: Boundary data is validated
rules.summary: External input should be parsed at transport, persistence, job, and integration boundaries before it reaches feature logic.
rules.rationale: Feature code should work with known shapes; uncertainty belongs at the edge.
examples: Route parses request body before calling feature service
antiPatterns: Repeated unknown coercion inside domain logic
Components defensively handle every possible server shape

rules.title: Validation lanes are declared
rules.summary: Projects should declare fast local checks, targeted feature checks, and slower release checks so agents know what proof is proportional to a change.
rules.rationale: Without lanes, agents either over-run expensive checks or under-prove risky work.
examples: typecheck and unit test as fast lane
E2E and build as release lane
Feature-specific commands listed in project docs
antiPatterns: Only one broad CI command is documented
Agent must guess which test proves a UI or API change

rules.title: Generated artifacts have owners
rules.summary: Generated files must name their source or generator and should not be hand-edited as a shortcut.
rules.rationale: Generated drift is one of the fastest ways for agents to create confusing false truth.
examples: Generated docs point to the source command
AGENTS.md names generated paths and regeneration command
antiPatterns: Patch generated output directly
Generated folder has no ownership or refresh command
